reference.text: Most question words that start with wh are pronounced /w/ (what, when, where, which, why). But in who and whose the w is silent and they start with /h/: who /huː/, whose /huːz/.

reference.text: When the question word (Who?, What?, Which?, How many?, etc.) is the subject of the verb in the question, we don’t use an auxiliary verb (do / does / did): Who painted The Milkmaid? In most other questions in the present and past simple we use the auxiliary verb do / does / did + the infinitive: What music do you like?

reference.wrong: Who did paint The Milkmaid? / What music you like?
reference.right: Who painted The Milkmaid? / What music do you like?
reference.why: No auxiliary when the question word is the subject; with an object question you need do / does / did.

tasks.instruction: Your English course. Ask and answer the questions
tasks.note: SB 1d «Ask and answer the questions with a partner» → разговор с ИИ по 10 вопросам из 1c

exercises.situation: A friendly end-of-course chat in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). Ask the student some of these questions about their English course, one at a time, and answer when they ask you: How do you usually get to class? Who do you usually sit next to? What are you going to do after this class? How many different teachers have you had since you started learning English? In your class, whose pronunciation do you think is the best? How often have you missed a class? If you could go to an English-speaking country on holiday, where would you go? When would your ideal time be to have English classes? Which do you find more difficult, speaking or listening? Are you going to carry on with English? Why (not)? After four or five questions, say ‘Now you ask me!’. If the student makes a mistake with question words or word order in questions, repeat the correct form naturally in your reply.
exercises.goal: Answer questions about your English course and ask some back.
exercises.opener: Hi! We’re almost at the end of the course. So, how do you usually get to class – on foot, by car, or on public transport?
criteria: answers at least five questions in full sentences
asks at least three questions with the correct question word
uses the correct word order in questions (question word + auxiliary + subject + verb)
gives a reason with because at least once

steps.text: Answer questions about how you study
steps.example: I usually come by bus. I sit next to my friend Olga.

steps.text: Say what you find more difficult
steps.example: I find listening more difficult because people speak very fast.
Where would you go on holiday? Which do you find more difficult? How often have you missed a class?

steps.text: Say if you’re going to carry on with English
steps.example: Yes, I’m going to carry on because I need English for my job.

tasks.instruction: General knowledge quiz. Ask your questions and answer your partner’s
tasks.note: SB 3 + Communication quiz A/B b–c (задать свои вопросы партнёру, ответить на его, посчитать баллы) → разговор с ИИ: ученик задаёт вопросы квиза A, ИИ задаёт вопросы квиза B

exercises.situation: A general knowledge quiz game in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). The student is Student A and asks you their questions (they have three options for each: e.g. Who lost the battle of Waterloo in 1815? Napoleon; Which American actor starred in The Martian? Matt Damon; Who wrote the songs in Mamma Mia? Abba; Which Formula One driver won his first world championship in 2008? Lewis Hamilton; Which famous Roman said ‘I came, I saw, I conquered’? Julius Caesar; Who broke the world record for the 100 and 200 metres in Beijing in 2008? Usain Bolt; Which painter cut off part of his ear? Van Gogh; Who discovered penicillin? Alexander Fleming). Answer their questions, sometimes right and sometimes wrong. Then ask your questions, one at a time, each with three options: Who became President of the USA eight years after his father had been president? (Bill Clinton / Barack Obama / George Bush – George Bush); Who played Hermione Granger in the Harry Potter films? (Emma Watson / Carey Mulligan / Kate Winslet – Emma Watson); Which sport became an Olympic sport in 2016? (golf / handball / volleyball – golf); Who painted the Sistine Chapel? (Leonardo da Vinci / Michelangelo / Raphael – Michelangelo); Who wrote The Da Vinci Code? (Stephen King / John Grisham / Dan Brown – Dan Brown); Who used a wooden horse to enter the city of Troy? (the Greeks / the Romans / the Persians – the Greeks); Which famous boxer refused to fight in the Vietnam War in 1967? (Muhammad Ali / Joe Frazier / Sugar Ray Robinson – Muhammad Ali); Who invented the telephone? (Marconi / Bell / Stephens – Bell). Say if each answer is right and keep the score. At the end, say who got the most correct answers. If the student asks a subject question with did (Who did paint…?), repeat it correctly.
exercises.goal: Ask your quiz questions correctly and answer the teacher’s questions.
exercises.opener: Let’s play! You’re Student A. Ask me your first question – remember to give me three options.
criteria: asks at least five quiz questions correctly without an auxiliary (Who lost…? Which painter cut…?)
gives the three options for each question
says if the teacher’s answers are right or wrong
answers the teacher’s questions in full sentences (I think Bell invented the telephone.)

steps.text: Ask your first question with three options
steps.example: Who lost the battle of Waterloo in 1815? The Duke of Wellington, Bismarck, or Napoleon?

steps.text: Say if the answer is right
steps.example: That’s right! / Sorry, that’s wrong – it was Napoleon.
I think Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel.
I got six answers right and you got five, so I won!

reference.title: File 11
reference.text: used to / didn’t use to + infinitive for past habits and states: I used to have long hair. Did you use to…? might / might not + infinitive for possibility: I might buy her a ring. She might not come. so / neither + auxiliary + I to say that you are the same: A I love travelling. B So do I. A I can’t do this. B Neither can I.

reference.title: File 12
reference.text: Past perfect (had / hadn’t + past participle) for an earlier past action: When I got to the station, the train had left. Reported speech: tenses move back (am → was, will → would, did / have done → had done); said (no person) / told + person. Subject questions have no auxiliary: Who lives next door? Other questions use do / does / did: Where did you buy that dress?

tasks.instruction: Can you understand this text? Read the two stories. What do they have in common?
tasks.note: Revise and Check 11&12 «Can you understand this text?» a → Blank. MODEL
tasks.context:
Stop the plane – we want to get on!

An Italian couple ran out onto the runway of Malta’s international airport to stop a Ryanair jet from leaving for Italy without them, a Maltese court heard on Thursday.

Matteo Clementi, 26, and Enrica Apollonio, 23, got stuck in terrible traffic on their way to the airport on Wednesday. When they arrived, the gate was closed and they were not allowed to board their flight back to Italy. They went to the next gate, forced open a security door, and ran towards the plane. The engines were running and the stairs had been removed, but the couple tried signalling to the pilots to let them get on. However, they were not allowed to board and were arrested by security staff.

A lawyer defending them in court said that Wednesday was Enrica’s 23rd birthday. She had wanted to celebrate it with her family and friends in Italy. Instead she spent the evening in prison, and the couple were fined €2,329.

From $20 to $1,000,000 in 30 minutes

A man who found $20 in the street near San Francisco International Airport used it to play the California lottery and won $1 million, lottery spokesman Greg Parashak said on Monday.

Hubert Tang used the $20 to buy two lottery scratch cards at a store near the airport on Wednesday and won the top prize with one of them, Parashak told us.

Tang said, ‘I scratched the ticket outside the store. I told my friend who I was with that I didn’t know if it was real but I thought I had just won a million dollars.’ Tang, who works as a barman at the airport, had not played the lottery for the last ten years. He said that he planned to continue working and had not decided how to spend the money. But he said that he might leave $20 notes in different places so that other people could find them and be lucky like him.

exercises.situation: A friendly revision chat in an English class (level: pre-intermediate) after Files 11 and 12. Check that the student can do these things, one by one, with short questions and reactions: 1) talk about three things they used to do when they were a child; 2) say two things they might do next week; 3) respond with so or neither to these sentences, said one at a time: ‘I like pop music.’, ‘I haven’t finished this exercise yet.’, ‘I’m going out tonight.’, ‘I didn’t know the answer.’ (they can agree or not: So do I / I don’t); 4) continue these sentences with the past perfect: ‘I got to the station, but…’ and ‘When I saw him I was surprised because…’; 5) report two things somebody said to them yesterday using said or told me; 6) ask you three questions without an auxiliary verb beginning with Who, How many and Which (answer them). Keep it natural, one thing at a time; if the student makes a mistake with used to, might, so / neither, the past perfect, reported speech or subject questions, repeat the correct form naturally in your reply.
exercises.goal: Show what you can say after Files 11 and 12.
exercises.opener: Hi! Let’s see what you remember from Files 11 and 12. First, tell me three things you used to do when you were a child.
criteria: uses used to / didn’t use to correctly for three childhood habits
says two plans with might / might not + infinitive
responds with so / neither + the right auxiliary
finishes both sentences with the past perfect
reports two things with said (that) / told me (that) and the tense moved back
asks three subject questions without do / does / did
